title: Probabilistic Synaptic Release
content_html:
Probabilistic Synaptic Release

→ Memory as Select – Change – Reconstruct

When an action potential arrives at a presynaptic bouton, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open. The local calcium nanodomain raises the probability (not certainty) that one or more docked, primed vesicles will fuse with the membrane via the SNARE complex, triggered by synaptotagmin acting as a Ca2+ sensor. Release occurs in quanta (vesicles), as shown by classic quantal analyses at neuromuscular synapses.

  • Quantal Postsynaptic responses are sums of discrete vesicle events.
  • Stochastic Ca2+ channel opening and molecular interactions are noisy.
  • Tunable Release probability (pr) and readily releasable pool size are modulated by activity and neuromodulators.

Select – Change – Reconstruct

Select

  • Which vesicles are docked & primed (state of vesicle pools).
  • Which Ca2+ channels open; local nanodomain geometry.
  • Neuromodulators set baseline pr (gain control).

Change

  • Short‑term plasticity (facilitation, depression, augmentation, PTP) changes pr within milliseconds–minutes.
  • Activity‑dependent vesicle depletion & replenishment reshape response statistics over time.

Reconstruct

  • Downstream circuits integrate noisy synaptic events into probabilistic population codes that support Bayesian inference during perception, recall, and decision.
  • Memory retrieval reads out a distribution, not a single fixed value → variability and bias become principled, not accidental.

Minimal generative model for a synapse

Binomial quantal model: EPSC = q · k, with k ∼ Binomial(N, pr)

  • N = number of release sites (or docked vesicles in the readily releasable pool).
  • pr = release probability per site, modulated by residual Ca2+ (facilitation) and depletion.
  • q = quantal size (postsynaptic response to one vesicle), itself variable.

Paired‑pulse ratio (PPR) inversely tracks baseline pr: low pr → facilitation (PPR>1); high pr → depression (PPR<1).

Consequences for memory

Encoding: Stochastic synapses sample inputs; variability spreads activity across ensembles, aiding generalisation.
Consolidation: Activity‑dependent changes in pr and pool dynamics bias which traces stabilise.
Retrieval: Population codes integrate noisy inputs; recall is inherently probabilistic, consistent with reconstructive memory and confidence distributions.

Bayesian brain frameworks formalise how variability supports near‑optimal inference and decision.
